newsitem.title: FRANCE: Guinness willing to up Moet stake - paper.
newsitem.headline: Guinness willing to up Moet stake - paper.

text.p: Guinness would be willing to raise its 34 percent stake in the drinks subsidiary of French group LVMH, Moet Hennessy, but not at any price, Guinness chairman Tony Greener said in an interview.

He also told the French weekly Journal des Finances, in the edition appearing on Saturday, that the cross-holdings between LVMH and Guinness are more balanced, in financial terms, since the sale last week by LVMH of seven percent of Guinness.
An advance copy of the interview was sent to Reuters on Friday.

Greener said Guinness bought back 2.3 percent because that was all it could buy. "LVMH sold a third of its stake to Goldman Sachs, which then placed the shares with around 100 international institutions. We bought what was offered to us, and we would have gone further if that were possible but there were too many demands," he said.
"The way the shares were placed and the fact that Guinness's stock wasn't affected show in any case the interest that our stock can attract," he said.
He said LVMH's move had effectively balanced the cross-holdings, with "the value of LVMH's stake in our capital roughly equivalent to that of our interests in Moet Hennessy."
Asked if Guinness would be interested in increasing its stake in Moet Hennessy, Greener replied: "The answer is yes, but not at any price".
"In any case, we have the right of first refusal for this business whose activities complement ours and which contributes substantially to our results," he said.

Greener said Guinness's shares have underperformed in part because of the rise of the British pound against other currencies -- a negative factor for a group which generates 90 percent of its turnover through exports.

Other factors weighing on the share include Guinness's heavy investment outlays in the initial stages of its drive to boost its presence in new markets, in Asia for example, and the fact that investors are not aware how successful the group is, he said.
"In the last five years, we have generated cashflow, before dividends, of more than two billion pounds," he said.
Greener said he did not see advantages to de-merging the group, whose divisions were complementary and balanced in terms of growth.

"We don't see what advantages we could draw from such an operation, even if we have, for a time, studied such an option among others," he said. He said the group's share buyback plans aimed to raise the share price.
